questions.question: The school garden has 4 rows of carrot plants. Each row has exactly 16 plants, and there are no other plants. How many carrot plants are in the garden altogether?
questions.explain: Equal rows of the same size means you join 4 groups of 16, so multiply: 4 × 16 = 64. The word ‘each’ makes many students divide, but nothing is being shared out here — the groups are being put together.

questions.question: A library in Burnaby has 72 new books. The librarian puts the same number of books on each of 8 shelves, using all the books. How many books go on one shelf?
questions.explain: One whole amount (72) is being split into 8 equal shelves, so divide: 72 ÷ 8 = 9. Words like ‘in all’ or ‘total’ tempt students to multiply, but the total is already given — you are finding the size of one part.

questions.question: A farm stand has 96 apples. The worker fills bags with exactly 8 apples in every bag until all the apples are used. How many bags does the worker fill?
questions.explain: You know the whole (96) and the size of each group (8), so divide to find how many groups: 96 ÷ 8 = 12. Seeing two numbers and the word ‘every’ often makes students multiply, but here the 96 apples are being broken apart, not built up.

questions.question: Twenty-four students are going on a field trip to the aquarium. Every student pays the same fee of $8. How much money does the class collect in total?
questions.explain: There are 24 equal amounts of $8, so multiply: 24 × 8 = $192. The word ‘every’ does not mean divide — ask yourself whether you are collecting many equal groups (multiply) or splitting one amount (divide).

questions.question: Chloe has 135 candies for her birthday party. She puts exactly 5 candies in each treat bag and uses every candy. Which number sentence finds how many treat bags she fills?
questions.explain: The 135 candies are the whole, and 5 is the size of each group, so divide: 135 ÷ 5 = 27 bags. Choosing multiplication because of the words ‘each bag’ gives 675, which is more candies than Chloe ever had — always check whether your answer makes sense.

questions.question: A Grade 4 class of 27 students is going canoeing on Deer Lake. Each canoe can carry at most 4 students. How many canoes are needed so that every student gets a seat?
questions.explain: Divide to see how many groups of 4 fit: 27 ÷ 4 = 6 with a remainder of 3, and those 3 students still need a boat, so 7 canoes are needed. Multiplying because of ‘each canoe’ gives 108, and dropping the remainder leaves 3 students on shore.

questions.question: A rectangular garden bed at the community centre covers an area of 96 square metres. One side of the bed measures 6 metres. How long is the other side?
questions.explain: Area is found by multiplying the two sides, so when the area and one side are known you divide: 96 ÷ 6 = 16 metres. Multiplying the two given numbers gives 576, which would be the area of a much bigger bed, not a side length.

questions.question: A community centre sets up 144 chairs in rows, with 8 chairs in every row and no chairs left over. Jayden says the words ‘rows of 8’ mean he should multiply. Which statement is correct?
options: 144 ÷ 8 = 18 rows, because the 144 chairs are split into equal rows of 8
questions.explain: The 144 chairs are the whole being broken into equal rows of 8, so divide: 144 ÷ 8 = 18 rows. Picking the operation from a keyword like ‘of’ instead of from the situation gives 1152 rows, far more rows than there are chairs.

questions.question: A school orders 8 boxes of skipping ropes with 15 ropes in each box. All of the ropes are then shared equally among 5 classes. How many ropes does each class get?
questions.explain: Multiply to find the total ropes, 8 × 15 = 120, then divide to share them out, 120 ÷ 5 = 24 ropes per class. The word ‘each’ appears in both steps, so decide by the situation: boxes are being combined, then the total is being split.

questions.question: Mira has 150 beads. She uses exactly 7 beads for every bracelet and makes as many complete bracelets as she can. How many complete bracelets does she make, and how many beads are left over?
questions.explain: Divide the whole by the group size: 150 ÷ 7 = 21 with a remainder of 3, since 21 × 7 = 147 and 150 − 147 = 3. A leftover of 7 is impossible because 7 more beads would make one more bracelet, and multiplying 150 × 7 answers a different question entirely.

questions.question: Which one of these problems is solved by the calculation 96 ÷ 4?
options: There are 96 stickers in each of 4 albums. How many stickers are there in all?
A jar holds 96 marbles and 4 more marbles are dropped in. How many marbles are in the jar now?
A camp has 96 juice boxes packed equally into 4 coolers. How many juice boxes are in one cooler?
Ella has 96 hockey cards and gives 4 of them to her cousin. How many cards does she keep?
questions.explain: Division fits when one whole amount is split into equal parts, which is what happens to the 96 juice boxes going into 4 coolers. The stickers problem also has 96 and 4 with the word ‘each’, but there 4 equal groups are being joined, so it needs multiplication.
